column2: So take up what is auspicious; let there be no despondency in you, Achyuta; slay your foes, protect the subjects and cherish the twice-born.
Facing him on a seat covered with a fine coverlet, Satyaki and Vasudeva, subduers of foes, sat down.
Placing the king in the middle, Bhimasena and Arjuna, both great souls, sat on two smooth jewelled seats.
On a bright, gold-adorned couch-seat, Pritha (Kunti) sat with Sahadeva and Nakula.
Sudharma, Vidura, Dhaumya and the Kaurava Dhritarashtra sat separately on seats like flames.
Yuyutsu, Sanjaya and the renowned Gandhari—wherever King Dhritarashtra was, there all sat.
Seated there, the righteous one touched white flowers, svastika signs, unhusked grain, earth, gold, silver and jewels.
Then all the subjects, putting the household priest in front, saw the king of dharma, bringing abundant auspicious things:
earth, gold, jewels of many kinds, and the vessels for consecration filled with all the materials.
They consecrated Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, as lord of the earth, with the royal sage Dhritarashtra and all the subjects.
Then they had the drums, tabors and kettledrums sounded, and the king of dharma accepted all that duly.
Of abundant fees, he honoured them duly, and then with a thousand nishkas had Brahmanas pronounce blessings, those versed in Vedic study and endowed with good conduct.
Those pleased Brahmanas, O king, said "Hail" and "Victory", and crying like swans praised Yudhishthira:

Yudhishthira, mighty-armed Pandava, by good fortune you have won; by good fortune you have gained your own dharma by valour, greatly radiant one.
mahabharata:12:40.20	By good fortune the wielder of Gandiva and Bhimasena the Pandava, and you, O king, are well, and the two Pandavas, sons of Madri.
mahabharata:12:40.21	Freed, hero, from this destruction, from the battle, your foes slain, quickly do the later duties, Pandava.
Then, honoured by the good, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, took up the great kingdom with his friends, Bharata.

Fortunate are the sons of Pandu in the world, for whom the best of Brahmanas, assembled, speak of virtues, whether true or untrue.
mahabharata:12:41.3	I think we are surely to be favoured by you, since, free of envy, you speak of us as endowed with such virtues.
mahabharata:12:41.4	King Dhritarashtra, our father, is our supreme deity; those who wish to please me must remain in his pleasure and in his food.
mahabharata:12:41.5	For this I live, having made the great slaughter of kinsmen: I must serve him constantly, untiring.
mahabharata:12:41.6	If I am to be favoured by you, my friends, then you ought to behave toward Dhritarashtra as before.
mahabharata:12:41.7	He is the lord of the world, and of you and me; to him belongs the whole earth and all the Pandavas; you should hold this word of mine in mind.
Having dismissed all the townsfolk and country folk, saying "Follow the king as you wish", the delight of the Kurus appointed Bhimasena as heir-apparent.
For counsel, decision, and consideration of the six measures of policy, he gladly appointed the wise Vidura.
For knowing what is done and not done, and for considering income and expenditure, he appointed Sanjaya, prosperous and rich in qualities.
For estimating the strength of the army and the pay and rations, the king appointed Nakula, and for supervising workmen.
For checking enemy armies and crushing the proud, King Yudhishthira appointed Phalguna.
For the Vedic affairs of the twice-born and other duties he appointed Dhaumya, best of priests, scorcher of foes.
He appointed Sahadeva ever close by, for by him the king was guarded in all conditions, lord of men.
Whomever he thought fit for whatever tasks, to those he assigned them, the king being pleased.
The righteous king, slayer of heroes, devoted to dharma, said to Vidura, Sanjaya and the great-minded Yuyutsu:

Whatever must be done for my father the king, rising each time, all of it must be done by you with care, as it should be.
mahabharata:12:41.18	And whatever tasks there are daily for the townsfolk and country folk, those are to be done by dharma with the king's permission.
King Dhritarashtra gave the funeral rites for his sons, with food, cows, wealth and wondrous costly jewels, rich in all desires, the greatly renowned one.
Yudhishthira, with Draupadi, gave for Karna, Drona, Dhrishtadyumna, Abhimanyu and the Rakshasa son of Hidimba,
and for Virata and the other friends who had helped, for Drupada and the sons of Draupadi.
To thousands of Brahmanas, naming each separately, he gave wealth, garments, jewels and cows, and satisfied them.
And for whichever other lords of the earth had no friends, naming them each, the king performed the funeral rites.
The Pandava had halls, water-sheds and various reservoirs made for the funeral rites of all friends.
Having become free of debt to them and gone to the worlds free of reproach, the king did his duty, protecting the people by dharma.
He honoured Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura as before, and all the Kaurava ministers and servants.
With houses, clothing and food for the wretched, blind and poor, the king, intent on kindness, showed favour.
Having conquered the whole earth and become free of debt to his enemies, Yudhishthira ruled happily, rivalless.
[Yudhishthira said:] "By your grace, Krishna, and by policy and strength, wisdom and valour, bull of the Yadus,
this kingdom of my father and grandfather has been regained by me. Homage to you, lotus-eyed, again and again, subduer of foes.
They call you the one Purusha, they call you lord of the Satvatas; great sages praise you by many names.
Homage to you, Vishvakarman, soul of the universe, source of the universe, Vishnu, Jishnu, Hari, Krishna, Vaikuntha, best of men.
In the ancient time you lay seven nights in Aditi's womb; you alone are the son of Prishni; they call you of the three ages.
You are called Shuchishrava, Hrishikesha, Ghritarchis, Hamsa, Trichakshu, Shambhu, the One, Vibhu and Damodara.
Varaha, Agni, Brihadbhanu, Vrishana, the one marked with Tarkshya, Anikasaha, Purusha, Shipivishta, Urukrama,
Vachishtha, Ugra, Senani, Satya, Vajasani, Guha, Achyuta, Chyavana, Sankriti and Vikriti of the foes, Vrisha.
Savishtakrit, Bhishaj, Avarta, Kapila and Vamana; Yajna, Dhruva, Patanga and Jayatsena you are called.
Shikhandin, Nahusha, Babhru, Divaspriś, Punarvasu, Subabhru, Uksha, Rukma, Sushena and Dundubhi.
Gabhastinemi, Shripadma, Pushkara, Pushpadharana, Ribhu, Vibhu, the subtlest of all, and the Savitra you are recited.
You are the ocean, Brahma, the purifying abode, the bow; they call you Hiranyagarbha; Svadha and Svaha, Keshava.

You are the womb and dissolution of this, Krishna; you alone create this universe in the beginning, and this universe is in your power, womb of the universe; homage to you, wielder of Sharnga, discus and sword.
Thus praised by the king of dharma, Krishna, the lotus-eyed, pleased in the midst of the assembly, the best of the Yadus, welcomed the eldest Pandava of the Bharata line with abundant words.
Then King Yudhishthira, wise, consoling Bhima of terrible valour, Arjuna and the twins, said:

You, with your bodies cut by various weapons of your enemies in the great battle, were wearied and greatly tormented by grief and anger.
mahabharata:12:44.4	You, best of men, endured painful dwelling in the forest for my sake, as base men would.
mahabharata:12:44.5	Let this victory be enjoyed as you please and at your ease; rested, with understanding regained, you will meet me again tomorrow.
[Vaishampayana said:] "Hear attentively, king, pure and composed, the departure from the body of the great-souled Bhishma, tiger of the Kurus.
As soon as the sun had turned to the north, he concentrated himself in himself, composed.
Like the sun with scattered rays, Bhishma, covered with hundreds of arrows, lay surrounded by supreme splendour and the best of Brahmanas,
by Vyasa, Vedashravas, the divine sage Narada, Devasthana, Vatsya, and Ashmaka and Sumantu,
and by these and other greatly fortunate great-souled bands of sages, with faith, restraint and honour, like the moon among planets.
But Bhishma, tiger among men, lying on his bed of arrows, in deed, mind and speech meditated on Krishna, standing with joined palms.
In a voice full and resounding he praised Madhusudana, lord of yoga, Padmanabha, Vishnu, Jishnu, lord of the world.
With joined palms, pure, the best of speakers, Bhishma, supremely righteous, then praised the lord Vasudeva.
In whom all beings stand and into whom they enter, the qualities in the lord of beings, like jewels on a thread,
in whom, the eternal, extended thread, the universe, existent and non-existent, is strung like a garland, whose body is the universe and who is the maker of the universe,
Hari of a thousand heads, a thousand feet and eyes, they call Narayana, the god who is the final refuge of the universe.
Subtler than the subtle, vaster than the vast, weightier than the weighty, best of the best,
whom they sing in the vakyas, anuvakyas, nishads and Upanishads, whose deeds are true, the truth among truths, among the Samans,
the fourfold-souled one by the four, abiding in sattva, lord of the Satvatas, whom they worship as god with divine secret supreme names,
whom the goddess Devaki bore to Vasudeva to protect the earthly Brahma, as the fire-stick bears blazing fire,
whom the single-minded, free of desire, having sacrificed for endlessness, see as Govinda, the Self free of stain, established in himself,
called Purusha in the Puranas, Brahma at the beginnings of ages, Sankarshana at the dissolution—him, the one to be worshipped, we worship.
Beyond the deeds of Wind and Indra, beyond the splendour of sun and fire, beyond intellect, senses and mind—him, the Prajapati, I take refuge in.
Whom they call maker of the universe, lord of the moving and unmoving, overseer of the world, the imperishable, the supreme station,
golden-hued, whom Aditi bore as an embryo, destroyer of Daityas, who being one was born in twelve forms—homage to him, the Self as Sun.
Who in the bright fortnight satisfies the gods and in the dark the ancestors with nectar, and who is king of the twice-born—homage to him, the Self as Moon.
Beyond the great darkness, the person blazing in splendour, knowing whom one passes beyond death—homage to him, the Self as the knowable.
Whom the hosts of Brahmanas sing as great in the Brihati verse, in the fire, in the great sacrifice—homage to him, the Self as the Veda.
Whose abode is the Rik, Yajus and Saman, whose form is the ten-and-a-half oblation, whom they extend with seven threads—homage to him, the Self as sacrifice.
Who as the Suparna, whose name is the Yajus, whose metre is his body, the Trivrit his head, the Rathantara and Brihat his eyes—homage to him, the Self as hymn.
Who was born at the thousand-year sacrifice as the sage of the creators of the universe, the golden-hued bird—homage to him, the Self as swan.
Whose feet are limbs, whose joints are sections, marked with vowels and consonants, whom they call the imperishable eternal—homage to him, the Self as speech.
Who builds the bridge of the good by truth, the source of nectar, by the limbs of conduct in dharma and wealth—homage to him, the Self as truth.
Whom those who follow dharma separately, seeking the fruits of dharma separately, worship by separate dharmas—homage to him, the Self as dharma.
Him whom the great sages seek, the unmanifest in the manifest, the knower of the field seated in the field—homage to him, the Self as the field.
Whom the Sankhyas call the seventeenth, the Self of sight abiding in the self, covered with sixteen qualities—homage to him, the Self as Sankhya.
Whom the sleepless, who have conquered breath, abiding in sattva with senses restrained, see as light as they practise yoga—homage to him, the Self as yoga.
To whom, at the cessation of merit and demerit, the fearless, tranquil renouncers go, free of rebirth—homage to him, the Self as liberation.
He who at the end of a thousand ages, as blazing fire, devours beings—homage to him, the dreadful Self.
Who, having devoured all beings and made the world a single ocean, sleeps alone as a child—homage to him, the Self as illusion.
Homage to that Purusha of a thousand heads and immeasurable self, whose sleep is yoga through the cycle of the four oceans.
In the navel of the Unborn, in whom the universe is established, the lotus of the lotus-eyed one—homage to him, the Self as lotus.
In whose hair are the clouds, in the joints of whose limbs are the rivers, in whose belly the four oceans—homage to him, the Self as water.
Who revolves through the ages in his parts, in days, seasons and years, the maker of creation and dissolution—homage to him, the Self as Time.
Whose mouth is the Brahmana, whose arms are the kshatriya, whose thighs and belly the Vaishya, and in whose feet the Shudras rest—homage to him, the Self as the classes.
Whose mouth is fire, whose head is the sky, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye the sun, whose ears the quarters—homage to him, the Self as the world.
Him whom they call the guardian of objects for those who move among objects, by particular qualities—homage to him, the guardian Self.
Made of food, drink and fuel, increasing savour and life, who sustains beings—homage to him, the Self as breath.
Beyond Time, beyond sacrifice, beyond the existent and non-existent, without beginning, the beginning of the universe—homage to him, the Self as universe.
Who bewilders beings with the bonds of affection and attachment, for the preservation of creation—homage to him, the Self as delusion.
Knowing this knowledge of the Self, abiding in the five, which the knowers attain—homage to him, the Self as knowledge.
To him of immeasurable body, with eyes endless on every side, unlimited and immeasurable—homage to him, the Self to be contemplated.
To the matted, staff-bearing, big-bellied embodied one, with a water-pot and quiver—homage to him, the Self as Brahma.
To the trident-bearing lord of the thirty gods, Tryambaka, the great soul, whose sign is smeared with ash and raised—homage to him, the Self as Rudra.
To him who is the soul of the five elements, the end of beings and their beginning, free of anger, harm and delusion—homage to him, the tranquil Self."
You are Death and also the cause in the destruction of this creature; I think both are causes; not a cause, not without a cause.
There is wealth, Partha, lying on the Himalaya, abandoned by Brahmanas at the sacrifice of King Marutta; fetch it, son of Kunti; it will be enough.
These two arms of mine, smeared with sandal, are worthy of homage, by which Duryodhana was brought to ruin with his sons and kinsmen.
Seeing them settled, Uddhava, knower of yoga and skilled in aims, took leave of those heroes and went at the end of Sandura.
When that tiger among men, of Shakra's splendour, had fallen and was dying, Bhima, the invincible, said to the king:
We, Partha, bull among men, after a long time shall find comfort, seeing you, best of kings.
Then Duryodhana's house, adorned with palaces, filled with many jewels and crowded with maidservants and menservants,
permitted by Dhritarashtra and given by his brother, mighty-armed Vrikodara received, as Maghavan received Mandara.
And like Duryodhana's house, Duhshasana's too, with garlands of palaces and fearsome golden arches,
full of maids and menservants, rich in wealth and grain, mighty-armed Arjuna received by the king's command.
He gave it to the ever-pleasing Sahadeva, who rejoiced to receive it like the lord of wealth in Kailasa.
Yuyutsu, Vidura, the greatly radiant Sanjaya, Sudharma and Dhaumya went each to their own homes.
Shauri (Krishna), the tiger among men, with Satyaki entered Arjuna's dwelling like a tiger a mountain cave.
There, supplied with food and drink, comfortably lodged and awakened in comfort, they waited on King Yudhishthira.
Great sage, you ought to tell what the heroic revered Hrishikesha, the supreme teacher of the three worlds, did.
[Vaishampayana said:] "Hear, king of kings, as I truly tell it, blameless one, what the Pandavas did with Vasudeva at their head.
Having gained the kingdom, the greatly radiant king of dharma Yudhishthira established the four classes duly each in its own dharma.
The Pandava had a thousand nishkas pronounced for each of a thousand great-souled Brahmanas who had completed their studies.
Likewise he satisfied with desired things his dependants, servants, guests, and the wretched and even the logicians.
To the household priest Dhaumya he gave tens of thousands of cows, wealth, gold, silver and garments of many kinds.
To Kripa, great king, he behaved as to a teacher, and to Vidura the righteous one, strict in vow, paid honour.
With various food and drink, garments, beds and seats, the best of givers satisfied all his dependants.
Having brought about peace, that king, best of kings, honoured Yuyutsu, the son of Dhritarashtra, of great fame.
Having entrusted the kingdom to Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura, King Yudhishthira lived as if at ease.
Having thus pleased the whole city, Janamejaya, he went with joined palms to the great-souled Vasudeva.
Then on a great couch adorned with jewels and gold he saw Krishna seated, dark like a rain-cloud on Meru,
blazing with his body, adorned with divine ornaments, wrapped in yellow silk, like a jewel set in gold,
shining with the Kaustubha jewel on his chest, like the risen sun upon the mountain of dawn, crowned, for whom there is no comparison in the three worlds.
Approaching the great soul Vishnu in human form, he spoke sweetly with a smile at the start:

Has your night passed happily, best of the wise? Are all your knowledges serene, Achyuta?
mahabharata:12:45.18	Relying on that goddess, your wisdom, best of the wise, we have obtained the kingdom and the earth is in our power.
mahabharata:12:45.19	By your grace, revered one, who stepped across the three worlds, victory is gained and the highest fame, and we have not fallen from dharma.
To Yudhishthira the king of dharma speaking thus, the revered one said nothing, but fell into meditation.

Having taken the fourth path of meditation, best of men, you have gone far, god; therefore my mind is astonished.
mahabharata:12:46.3	Your breath of five functions, dwelling in the body, is restrained; all your senses are placed in the mind.
mahabharata:12:46.4	Your senses and mind are set in the intellect, and the whole host is placed in the divine knower of the field in you.
mahabharata:12:46.5	Your hairs do not stir, your intellect and mind are steady; you are like a post, a wall, a stone, motionless, Madhava.
mahabharata:12:46.6	As a lamp in a windless place burns unflickering, Achyuta, so are you, revered god, motionless, firm in resolve.
mahabharata:12:46.7	If I deserve to hear it here and it is not secret, cut my doubt, god, for I take refuge and entreat you.
mahabharata:12:46.8	You are doer and undoer, you the perishable and imperishable, without beginning or end, the first, you alone are the best of men.
mahabharata:12:46.9	To me who have taken refuge in you, a devotee bowing my head, explain the truth of this meditation, best of upholders of dharma.

I have gone in mind to him by whom, rushing swiftly against the whole circle of kings, three maidens were carried off long ago.
mahabharata:12:46.14	Who fought Bhargava for twenty-three days and was not overcome by Rama—I have gone to him in mind.
mahabharata:12:46.15	Whom Ganga bore as a king by the rite of conception, a pupil of Vasishtha, dear one—I have gone in mind to him, king.
mahabharata:12:46.16	Who, greatly radiant and wise, bears the divine weapons and the four Vedas with their limbs—I have gone to him in mind.
mahabharata:12:46.17	Rama's dear pupil, son of Jamadagni's disciple, Pandava, the support of all learning—I have gone to him in mind.
mahabharata:12:46.18	Uniting the host of senses and restraining the mind by intellect, he took refuge in me, and so my mind has gone to him.
mahabharata:12:46.19	He knows the past, the future and the present, bull among men, best of upholders of dharma; therefore my mind has gone to him.
mahabharata:12:46.20	When that tiger among men has gone to heaven by his own deeds, the earth, Partha, will be like a night without a moon.
mahabharata:12:46.21	So, Yudhishthira, go to Bhishma son of Ganga, of terrible valour, approach him, embrace his feet and ask what is in your mind.
mahabharata:12:46.22	Ask him, lord of the earth, of the four Vedas, the four hotri priests, the four stages of life, and the dharma of the four classes.
mahabharata:12:46.23	When that Bhishma, the bearer of the Kuru burden, has set, knowledge will become scanty; therefore I urge you.
Hearing Vasudeva's true, excellent words, the knower of dharma, his throat choked with tears, said to Janardana:

What you say of Bhishma's power, Madhava, I have no doubt of that, giver of honour.
mahabharata:12:46.26	The great fortune and power of Bhishma the great soul I have heard from great-souled Brahmanas as they spoke.
mahabharata:12:46.27	And you are the maker of the worlds; what you say, slayer of Madhu, is a word not to be doubted, delight of the Yadus.
mahabharata:12:46.28	Since you have favoured me with your mind, Madhava, putting you in front, we shall see Bhishma.
mahabharata:12:46.29	When the revered Sun turns (in his northern course) he will go to the worlds; therefore the Kaurava deserves a sight of you, mighty-armed one.
mahabharata:12:46.30	For him, the sight of you, the first god, the perishable and the imperishable, would be a gain, for you are Brahma, a treasure made of it.
Hearing this word of the king of dharma, Madhusudana said to Satyaki at his side, "Have my chariot yoked."
Satyaki, going out, said to Daruka near Keshava, "Let Krishna's chariot be yoked."
Hearing Satyaki's quick words, Daruka reported to Achyuta, with joined palms, the excellent chariot adorned with gold, with parts made of emerald, crystal and sun-stone, its wheels bound in gold,
bright as the sun's rays, swift, adorned with various jewels, like a newly risen sun in splendour, with a banner marked with wondrous Tarkshya (Garuda) and flags,
well yoked with the best horses led by Sugriva and the army, swift as thought, with golden-adorned bodies, O lion among kings.
